title: Romance and Limits
author: Reynolds, John Mark
summary: John Mark Reynolds meditates on love as the most powerful and therefore most dangerous virtue—when twisted, the greatest goods become the source of greatest harm. Using Trollope's novel Sir Harry Hotspur of Humblethwaite, Reynolds shows how a good man's excessive love for family, name, and lineage introduces corruption he cannot then remove. The tragedy is not lack of love but love disproportionately applied, making the novel a Christian meditation on how charity misapplied becomes the source of catastrophe.
points: Love is the greatest human virtue and the most dangerous: twisted charity, misapplied love, does the deepest evil rather than the greatest good.
Trollope's genius was his willingness to deny readers the happy ending when characters make choices that don't deserve one—realistic narrative justice rather than sentimental resolution.
Sir Harry Hotspur's tragedy is caused not by his vices but by his virtues applied without wisdom: too much love of family, name, and land introduces corruption he cannot remove.
Christianity as a romance requires practicing love toward enemies—which in practice always fails; cataloging those failures helps future generations do better.
A woman so intent on performing the external form of wifely virtue that she became too passive to exercise genuine virtue illustrates how form and substance can tragically diverge.
quotes: Trollope knew that there were many causes for such errors in the brilliant, if emotionally brutal, Sir Harry Hotspur of Humblethwaite, he takes good values, cherished virtues that save many characters in his other books, and shows how they can go wrong.
The obvious solution is to marry the title to the money and have everyone live happily every after, but George Hotspur is a grifter, a liar, and a cad.
In many of his books, Anthony Trollope shows how essential such loves are for England, but in this book he shows how love can go wrong.
The father of the tragedy is a good man Sir Harry Hotspur who spawns a tragedy by loving his family, his name, and his land too much.
(Lord have mercy on me a sinner!) Just as hope can become a mere delusion, faith irrational, so love can be reduced to passions.
